heading.headingText: Buildings with a long attention span.

dek.text: We design houses, civic buildings, and adaptive reuse projects. Work that is specific to its site, slow to date, and built to last forty years or more.

p1.text: We are a studio of eleven people working out of a converted warehouse in the inner city. We take on five or six projects a year, which is about as many as we can do well. We do not do every project that comes our way and we never have.

p2.text: The studio was founded in 2003. The founding partners are still here. So is the same approach: start with the site, draw by hand, leave things alone when they do not need to be touched, and argue about details until the details get easier.

jcr:content.jcr:description: Meridian House. Private residence. Northern coastline. 2023.
jcr:content.jcr:title: Meridian House

dek.text: A house built to watch the horizon rather than compete with it.

p0.text: Meridian House sits on a rocky headland facing due north, with the water on three sides and the wind for company. The program is simple: a single-family home for a couple who had retired from the city and wanted to see weather coming.

p1.text: The plan is a long bar turned parallel to the coast, broken into three volumes connected by glazed passages. The middle volume holds the kitchen and the shared living space. The end volumes are bedrooms and a small studio. Every room faces the water.

p2.text: The structure is reclaimed timber over a cast concrete base. The roof pitches inland, catching runoff into a cistern that feeds the garden. The garden is indigenous grasses, unirrigated, because the client wanted to see what the land would do on its own.

jcr:content.jcr:description: Ashford Cultural Centre. Cultural institution. Town square, Ashford. 2022.
jcr:content.jcr:title: Ashford Cultural Centre

meta.text: Cultural institution. Town square, Ashford. 2022. Completed.

dek.text: A civic building that uses its courtyard harder than its rooms.

p0.text: The brief for Ashford was a modest civic building with a gallery, a 180-seat auditorium, and a cafe. What the town actually needed was a covered outdoor space big enough to hold a market or a wedding or a town meeting.

p1.text: The plan wraps the interior program around a central courtyard covered by a shallow timber roof, forty metres on a side. The roof is carried on eight tree columns. The interior rooms open onto the courtyard in good weather and close up in winter without much fuss.

p2.text: In the two years since it opened the courtyard has hosted a farmer's market, three funerals, nine weddings, the annual school play, and a protest about traffic on the main road. The gallery is nice. The auditorium is fine. The courtyard is the building.

jcr:content.jcr:description: Linden Residence. Private residence. Inner city, infill lot. 2021.
jcr:content.jcr:title: Linden Residence

meta.text: Private residence. Inner city, infill lot. 2021. Completed.

dek.text: An infill house on a narrow lot that borrows light from its neighbors.

p0.text: Linden sits on a lot five metres wide between two older brick houses. The constraint of the site forced the diagram: everything happens front-to-back, not side-to-side, and every room has to earn its borrowed light.

p1.text: The front of the house is a quiet brick facade that matches the street. The back opens entirely to a small garden with a high east-facing wall. The middle of the house is a full-height stair that doubles as a lightwell, pulling sun from the roof down to the kitchen. We spent more time on that stair than on any other part of the project.

p2.text: The owners have three children and a dog. The house works because we designed for the dog first.

jcr:content.jcr:description: Crestwood Pavilion. Public pavilion. Crestwood Park. 2020.
jcr:content.jcr:title: Crestwood Pavilion

dek.text: A small park pavilion the city asked us to build for $180k and finished under budget.

p0.text: Crestwood was a tight brief with a tight budget. The city needed a sheltered gathering space in an under-used park, with room for a farmer's market on weekends and nothing much the rest of the time. They wanted it built cheap and built fast.

p1.text: We chose a simple steel-frame canopy and timber in-fill, prefabricated offsite in sections that could arrive on a flatbed and be bolted together in a week. The shape is a shallow hip that catches afternoon shade on the west and sheds rain north into a swale.

p2.text: We came in at $167,000, six percent under the allocated budget, with the leftover money going to benches and a water fountain. It has been up for four years and nobody has complained about it once.

jcr:content.jcr:description: Blackrock Studio. Artist studio. Industrial district. 2019.
jcr:content.jcr:title: Blackrock Studio

dek.text: A painting studio carved out of a disused mechanical workshop.

p0.text: Blackrock started as a mechanical workshop in the 1940s and had been empty for eight years when a painter approached us about converting it. She had a small budget and a large north-facing wall with clerestory windows, and that was basically the whole brief.

p1.text: We did almost nothing to the exterior. Inside we stripped the mezzanine and added a high partition wall to separate a working area from a small office and wet room. The old hoist is still overhead. It does not do anything anymore but it looks great.

p2.text: The light at noon is better than any studio we have designed from scratch, because we could not have designed it from scratch. Sometimes the best move is to leave things alone and put the walls where they need to be.

jcr:content.jcr:description: Solano Bridge. Pedestrian bridge. River crossing, Solano district. 2024.
jcr:content.jcr:title: Solano Bridge

meta.text: Pedestrian bridge. River crossing, Solano district. 2024. In construction.

dek.text: A pedestrian bridge replacing the temporary one that has been up for seventeen years.

p0.text: Solano is a weathering-steel pedestrian bridge replacing a temporary wooden span that the city put up in 2007 as a quick fix and then forgot about. The brief was "something nicer than what is there now and something that will last forty years", which is a fine brief if you read it charitably.

p1.text: The structure is a single span, 34 metres, in a shallow truss with the handrails integrated into the top chord. The deck is larch planks, grooved, replaceable in sections. The whole thing sits on two small concrete abutments set back from the water's edge so the ecology of the bank does not get disturbed.

p2.text: Construction starts in early 2026 and should finish by the end of summer. We will post progress photos when we remember to.

jcr:content.jcr:description: Not nostalgia. The constraint of a pencil on paper is still the fastest way to think through a building.
jcr:content.jcr:title: Why we still draw by hand at the start of every project

heading.headingText: Why we still draw by hand at the start of every project

dek.text: Not nostalgia. The constraint of a pencil on paper is still the fastest way to think through a building.

p0.text: We use the same computer tools as everyone else. When it comes time to document a building we have the models, the BIM, the engineering coordination. That is not in question.

p1.text: But for the first four or five weeks of a project, before the consultants are on board and before the site has been properly measured, we work almost entirely in plan sketches, section studies, and the occasional small chipboard model. The reason is not nostalgia. It is that the pencil imposes a cost on every line. You have to commit to a move before you draw it, because undoing a pencil line is a minor defeat.

p2.text: That cost is what we are paying for. It is the reason the first conversation with a client goes better at a table with a sheet of tracing paper on it than it does at a screen. The sketch is slow enough to think with.

jcr:content.jcr:description: What the client asks for and what the client wants are rarely the same sentence.
jcr:content.jcr:title: The brief is never the actual brief

heading.headingText: The brief is never the actual brief

dek.text: What the client asks for and what the client wants are rarely the same sentence.

p0.text: Every project starts with a brief. Sometimes it is a formal document with program requirements and a budget, and sometimes it is a text message that says "we need more space". Either way it is almost never what the client actually wants.

p1.text: The actual want is underneath the brief, and our first job is to dig until we find it. Often it is a specific feeling, or a habit that the current space is blocking. For Meridian House it was "we want to see weather coming". For Ashford it was "the town needs somewhere to gather that is not a parking lot". Neither of those sentences was in the written brief.

p2.text: The trick, if it is a trick, is to ask about something they love in another building and then not change the subject. That is usually where the real program lives.

jcr:content.jcr:description: Some notes after the Blackrock conversion wrapped.
jcr:content.jcr:title: Working with an old building is a conversation, not a translation

heading.headingText: Working with an old building is a conversation, not a translation

dek.text: Some notes after the Blackrock conversion wrapped.

p0.text: Blackrock Studio wrapped last month and I have been thinking about what I would tell a younger version of myself about renovation work. There are two traps. The first is to try to hide the existing building under a layer of new material, as if the old structure were something to be corrected. The second is to make too big a deal about the old building, to treat every beam and bolt as a precious object that must be preserved.

p1.text: The middle path is something like a conversation. The old building has things to say, and so do you. You listen to it for a few weeks before you say anything back. Then you put up a wall where it needs to be, you leave a hoist overhead because it is beautiful, and you let the compromise be visible.

p2.text: A client once asked me what percentage of an old building we should keep in a renovation. I do not have a number. But the question is wrong. It is not about percentages. It is about which moves pay and which moves do not.

jcr:content.jcr:description: Founded 2003. Eleven people in a converted warehouse. Five or six projects a year.
jcr:content.jcr:title: Our Studio

dek.text: Founded 2003. Based in the inner city. Five or six projects a year, no more than we can do well.

p1.text: We believe architecture is a slow discipline. The work we are proudest of took a long time to design and longer to build. We try to protect that pace and not to apologize for it.

p2.text: Every project begins with a long walk around the site, a conversation with whoever will use the building, and about four weeks of hand drawing before we turn on a computer. The sketches are slow enough to think with, which is the point.

p3.text: We keep the studio at eleven people on purpose. Small is a commitment, not a stage we are passing through. At eleven we can sit together at lunch, and the principal is involved in every project from the first sketch to the day it opens.

The Ashford Cultural Centre competition is won three years later.</dd> <dt>2019</dt> <dd>Blackrock Studio opens. jcr:content.jcr:description: Residential, cultural and civic, adaptive reuse, and landscape work.

dek.text: A short list. We keep the practice narrow on purpose and we are happy to recommend other firms when a project is not a fit.

residential-body.text: New-build houses and significant renovations, from infill lots to coastline properties. We work at any scale that fits on a residential plan set.

cultural-and-civic-body.text: Small-to-mid-sized public buildings: libraries, community centres, galleries, pavilions. Most of these start as competitions and all of them start with a long walk around the site.

adaptive-reuse-body.text: Old buildings that want a second life. We are particular about what we take on here. If the old building has nothing to say we are usually not the right firm.

landscape-and-site-body.text: When a project needs it, we work with landscape architects from the first week. Increasingly we think of this as the same work, not a discipline we subcontract out.

p1.text: A typical project starts with an introductory meeting and a site walk, usually at no cost. If we are a good fit on both sides we do a short paid feasibility phase, which is where we figure out whether the project is worth doing and how much it is likely to cost.

p2.text: From there the phases are conventional: schematic design, design development, construction documents, bidding, construction administration. We run our side of the process with one project lead and the appropriate junior staff on each phase. The principal who signed your contract will still be looking at the drawings on the last day.

p3.text: If you would like to talk about a project, the contact page is the right place to start.

jcr:content.jcr:description: Start a conversation about a new project. The first call is free.

dek.text: We respond to every enquiry within a week. If you are considering a new project we would like to hear about it.

studio-body.text: Suite 3, converted warehouse building on the east side. Second door after the bakery.

hours-body.text: Monday to Friday, 9 to 6. We are almost always in the studio but we have a bad habit of not answering the door. Email first.

p1.text: The first conversation is free and it is the most important one. Tell us what you are thinking about, even if it is vague. What kind of project, what site you have in mind if any, what timeline you are working against. We will read it carefully and write back.

p2.text: We take on five or six projects a year. If the fit is wrong we will say so and suggest a studio we think would be better. That is not a polite brush-off. It is how we keep the practice worth doing.
